stops.title: The Fiat of Nazareth
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Nazareth to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Warm limestone village courtyard and rock-hewn grotto of Nazareth bathed in morning golden light.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Pilgrims descend into the ancient rock grotto preserved inside the Basilica of the Annunciation, where an inscription reads "Hic Verbum Caro Factum Est" (Here the Word was made flesh).
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Archaeologists discovered 2nd-century Judeo-Christian graffiti inside the Nazareth grotto reading "XE MARIA" ("Hail Mary")—one of the oldest Marian inscriptions on Earth.
stops.saintQuote: Behold, I am the handmaid of the Lord; may it be done to me according to your word.

stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Five members of Basil’s immediate household were canonized as saints, largely shaped by the wisdom of his eldest sister St. Macrina the Younger.
stops.saintQuote: A tree is known by its fruit; a man by his deeds.

stops.imageCaption: Lantern-lit stone cloisters of an ancient Anatolian hospital courtyard where loaves of bread are shared with the poor.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Historians recognize the Basiliad as the world’s first comprehensive public hospital complex, setting the blueprint for charitable healthcare across East and West.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: When the Arian Emperor Valens threatened Basil with confiscation, exile, and death, Basil calmly replied that he owned only a ragged cloak and a few books—and that the emperor’s threats meant nothing to a man who feared only God.
stops.saintQuote: The bread in your cupboard belongs to the hungry; the coat unused in your closet belongs to the one who needs it.

stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Albert is the only scholar of the Middle Ages to earn the title "the Great" during his own lifetime, celebrated across Europe as Doctor Universalis for mastering virtually every branch of known science and theology.
stops.saintQuote: The aim of natural science is not simply to accept the statements of others, but to investigate the causes that are at work in nature.

stops.title: Dominican Calling in Padua
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Patavium to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Warm ochre Venetian-style arches and sunlit courtyard of medieval Padua with botanical sketches and manuscripts.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Padua remains home to the world’s oldest surviving university botanical garden—a fitting echo of Albert, who authored Europe’s pioneering treatise on botany and plant anatomy.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Albert was the first scientist in history to isolate the chemical element arsenic (around 1250 AD) and accurately describe the photosynthetic sensitivity of silver nitrate centuries before photography!

stops.title: Mentoring the "Dumb Ox" in Paris
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across University of Paris to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Candlelit medieval stone lecture hall in Paris’s Latin Quarter filled with eager students and a towering young scholar taking notes.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Place Maubert in the heart of Paris’s 5th arrondissement still carries Master Albert’s name nearly eight centuries after his open-air lectures.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: When Thomas Aquinas died prematurely in 1274, the aged Albert walked all the way from Cologne to Paris on foot at age 77 just to defend his beloved student’s writings from critics!
stops.saintQuote: You call him the Dumb Ox, but his bellowing in doctrine will one day resound throughout the whole world.

hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: As the first German master of theology at the University of Paris, Albert attracted so many students that he had to lecture outdoors in a public square—still called Place Maubert ("Magister Albertus") today! Among his students sat a quiet, broad-shouldered Italian nicknamed the "Dumb Ox": St. Thomas Aquinas. Albert famously prophesied: "One day the bellowing of this ox will fill the whole world."

detectiveClues.headline: Fearless Witness at Piazza Navona

detectiveClues.clueText: Born into a prominent French political family in Grenoble, Philippine dreamed since childhood of sailing to the Americas. When the French Revolution shut down monasteries and sent priests into hiding, she risked her life sheltering hunted clergy and nursing prisoners before joining St. Madeleine Sophie Barat’s Society of the Sacred Heart.

hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: At seventy-two years old and frail in health, Philippine begged to join a new mission to the displaced Potawatomi Nation in Kansas. Too elderly to learn the Potawatomi language, she spent hours every single day kneeling motionless on the wooden chapel floor praying for them. The Potawatomi children quietly dropped tiny pebbles on her cloak to see if she ever moved—and named her Quah-kah-ka-num-ad: "The Woman Who Prays Always."

stops.title: Opening the Windows of the Church

stops.imageCaption: Radiant golden shafts of morning light streaming through the high windows of St. Peter’s Basilica onto hundreds of gathered bishops.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Inside St. Peter’s Basilica, pilgrims pause in affectionate prayer before the glass altar enshrining St. John XXIII—canonized together with St. John Paul II in 2014.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: On the opening night of Vatican II, standing at his window overlooking a sea of candlelight in St. Peter’s Square, he delivered his spontaneous "Moonlight Speech": "Go home, find your children, give them a hug, and tell them: this is the hug of the Pope!"
stops.saintQuote: I want to throw open the windows of the Church so that we can see out and the people can see in.
